Neonatal specimens of Centroscymnus crepidater, commonly known as the Longnose velvet dogfish, emerge from their mothers at a total length of 30 centimeters [Lb = 30 centimeters]. This relatively modest birth size is typical of many deep-sea squaliform sharks, reflecting an extended period of yolk-dependent embryonic development within the maternal reproductive tract. Pregnant females captured off the coast of New Zealand have been documented with fully developed pups, with the gestation period occurring at the prevailing deep-sea temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. In these cold, stable benthic environments, the entire gestation lasts approximately 730 days [ab = approximately 730 days] at a temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. This exceptionally long gestational investment is among the most protracted recorded for any elasmobranch, a strategy that likely enhances neonatal survival in the food-limited mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones where the species resides. The pups are born fully developed and functionally independent, immediately capable of capturing small cephalopods and teleosts. Comparative data from closely related members of the Somniosidae family indicate that such an extended gestation and relatively large birth size are adaptations to the low metabolic demand and high pressure of the deep-sea environment, ensuring that offspring begin life with a considerable size advantage.

As individuals of Centroscymnus crepidater grow, their ultimate total length reaches 105 centimeters [Li = 105 centimeters] for females, while males capsize at a smaller maximum dimension of 93 centimeters [Li = 93 centimeters] in total length. This sexual dimorphism in ultimate size is a recurring pattern among deep-sea squaliforms, likely driven by the energetic demands of reproduction on females, who must accommodate developing embryos over their elongated gestation. A mature female specimen exhibiting this length can attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 10,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 10,100 grams], a substantial mass for a shark of this modest length. Mature males, in contrast, achieve a maximum wet weight of roughly 6,900 grams [Wwi = roughly 6,900 grams]. These body sizes represent the endpoints of growth trajectories that span several decades, with individuals likely ceasing length increase after reaching sexual maturity. Such growth patterns are typical of elasmobranchs that invest heavily in somatic and gonadal tissue rather than rapid body elongation, with the majority of resources allocated to maintaining condition in an environment where prey encounters are irregular.

The onset of reproductive capability in this species is marked by puberty, a developmental stage that occurs at different sizes between the sexes. In females, puberty is typically attained at a total length of approximately 86 centimeters [Lp = approximately 86 centimeters], though some variation exists, with records ranging from 76 to 102 centimeters in total length. For males, the equivalent transition to a reproductively active state occurs at a smaller size, approximately 65.4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 65.4 centimeters] in total length, with an interquartile range spanning from 59 to 81 centimeters in total length. This disparity in size at sexual maturation between sexes is consistent with the ultimate size dimorphism observed in adults. These pubertal lengths are derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue taken from commercial bycatch taken in the deep-water trawl fisheries off southern Australia and New Zealand. At these deep-water habitats, ambient temperatures remain a constant 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C] throughout the year, reinforcing the slow pace of life for this species. Achieving sexual maturity at these sizes requires a considerable investment of time, on par with other deep-sea chondrichthyans.

Reproduction in Centroscymnus crepidater follows a remarkably slow schedule, even by deep-sea standards. Gravid females carry litters that typically consist of between 2 and 10 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 10 pups per litter]. The investment in each pup is considerable, as evidenced by the extended gestation. Furthermore, females do not reproduce annually; available evidence indicates that they produce only 1 litter every 3 years [F_R_i = 1 litter every 3 years]. This extremely low reproductive output, combined with the late age of sexual maturation, renders this species highly vulnerable to overfishing. The environmental conditions that dictate this slow tempo are the cold, deep waters of the continental slope and abyssal plain, where the temperature remains stable at 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C], driving low metabolic rates. This slow rate of reproduction is a classic life-history trait of many deep-sea chondrichthyans, reflecting the energy constraints imposed by low prey availability and cold temperatures. The maximum lifespan documented for Centroscymnus crepidater is quite extensive for a shark of its body size. Based on growth ring counts from vertebral centra, the oldest individuals are estimated to live for approximately 26.5 years [am = approximately 26.5 years] at a temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. This extended longevity is consistent with the species’ life-history strategy of delayed maturity, low fecundity, and an extended gestation period, all measured in the cold, energetically conservative environment of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. The protracted gestation of approximately 730 days [ab = approximately 730 days] is among the longest recorded for any elasmobranch, reflecting the stable, cold conditions that govern deep-sea reproductive strategies at a temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. Such a prolonged lifespan provides ample time for the few reproductive events that occur throughout a female’s life, thereby maintaining a stable population size despite low annual recruitment. Morphological studies of the vertebral bands indicate that growth is slow and steady, with little evidence of a pronounced growth spurt. This life-span estimate confirms that the species can persist for decades, a trait that also requires strong conservation management in regions where it is taken as bycatch in deep-sea fisheries.
